A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ReasoningGuard. The complete main texts and appendices are readable, including algorithms, equations, tables, and figures. Content can be matched despite substantial reformatting and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original defense, utility, efficiency, ablation, and human-evaluation results in Sections 3–4 and Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds attention-score analyses, robustness experiments, model-transfer tests, and guard-filter comparisons.

M1.justification: The core attention-sink identification, safety phrase, IAS ranking, and adaptive sampling procedure remain unchanged. v2 additionally evaluates ReasoningGuard combined with Llama Guard 3 or GuardReasoner, adding optional post-generation filtering to the inference pipeline (Appendix D.5.2, Table 15).

E1.justification: AdvBench, SorryBench, MMLU, GPQA Diamond, MATH500, and XSTest are retained. Attack-input scenarios change: automated AutoRAN replaces manually constructed H-CoT attacks, and cipher-based Mousetrap attacks are added. This extends adversarial conditions within the existing tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds evaluated RealSafe-R1, SafeKey, SAFEPATH-FT, and SAFEPATH-ZS comparisons, plus Llama Guard 3 and GuardReasoner filtering baselines. Gradient Cuff disappears. PPL remains in a narrower appendix comparison, while SafeDecoding is restricted to the 7B/8B models. These substantially change comparator membership.

E3.justification: v2 replaces the AdvBench Llama Guard classification metric with the proportion receiving GPT-4o harmfulness score 5, retaining mean GPT scores. It adds Phi-4 and Qwen3 model configurations, controlled IAS sampling and NF4-versus-unquantized experiments, and reasoning-length metrics. Its reported decoding policy also extends nucleus decoding beyond utility evaluations; these statements do not establish which experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses examine IAS–harmfulness associations, varied instructive/misleading/irrelevant safety phrases, quantization sensitivity, reasoning-length preservation, and combinations with guard filters. A mathematical utility case is added and the failure example is replaced. Existing window, sampling, scaling-factor, decoding, and phrase-component ablations are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v2 introduces Spearman rank-correlation estimation for reasoning lengths and IAS boxplots reporting distributional spread, means, and medians. These extend descriptive statistical reporting. Neither version reports repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive results for new comparators, attacks, and analyses, while removing detailed QwQ utility, jailbreak, and XSTest results. Retained entries also change: ReasoningGuard's R1-Llama-8B no-attack GPT harmfulness scores change from 1.02/1.00 in v1 Table 10 to 1.40/1.00 in v2 Table 17. Changed metrics and incompletely specified subsets prevent interpreting the overall revisions as matched performance gains.

T1.justification: The attention, sink-selection, IAS, and token-complexity mathematics are substantively retained. Last-layer notation clarifies implementation, and the added Spearman formulas explain a standard evaluation statistic. The new IAS-sufficiency discussion supplies an empirical interpretation, not a formal theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a lightweight, training-free safeguard using attention-guided safety reflection and sampling. The abstract broadens its explicit effectiveness claim from three attacks and seven safeguards to four attacks and nine safeguards; the introduction also extends the claimed model-family coverage.

C2.justification: v2 interprets high IAS as sufficient but unnecessary for safety, connects utility preservation with reasoning-length consistency, and explains complementary roles and streaming limitations of post-hoc filters. It also qualifies comparison coverage because of unavailable training data and computational limits. These substantially extend the scientific interpretation; the IAS sufficiency wording exceeds what the conditional observational analysis establishes.

D1.justification: v2 specifies last-layer attention, identifies 14B/32B models as quantized, documents IAS-analysis sampling and filtering, and supplies implementation/checkpoint references for added attacks and defenses. GPU hardware and task-time estimates are retained. Exact evaluation subset sizes and random seeds remain unspecified.

R1.justification: Section 2.3 shifts from a general jailbreak-defense taxonomy to LRM-specific training-based and training-free alignment, positioning ReasoningGuard against closely related SAFEPATH and SafeKey approaches. AutoRAN, GuardReasoner, and additional model references are introduced, while several general defense references are removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and experimental narrative receive broad paragraph-level revisions. v2 reorganizes the appendices around a dedicated IAS analysis, restructures utility and ablation subsections, adds a model-transferability section, and separates limitations and ethical considerations from their earlier locations.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. Figures 1–2 are reorganized, the radar chart and ablation panels are revised, and tables are restructured with comparator groups and average columns. New IAS boxplots, phrase-example tables, and analysis tables substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence for the central safety–utility claim through direct comparisons with closely related LRM alignment methods and guard models, addressing an important gap in v1. The IAS, phrase-robustness, quantization, and reasoning-length analyses also test important assumptions behind the method. Reduced QwQ reporting and overstrong IAS-sufficiency wording are drawbacks, and reproducibility remains incomplete, but the more relevant comparisons and targeted validation provide a substantial net improvement.
